insider_note: The unknown x sits without a derivative next to the dy term, which is the signal to treat this as linear IN x rather than forcing it into the usual dy/dx form; since Q turns out to be the first-degree polynomial y+1, a single integration by parts finishes the job.

steps.label: Rewrite as linear in x and identify P
steps.margin_note: One mark. Take the reciprocal of dy/dx to write the equation as linear in x.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever dy/dx = 1/(linear in x and y), invert it to dx/dy = (that same linear expression) — a fast route to a linear-in-x equation.
lines: which is linear D.E in x. Here P = −1
steps.why: Taking the reciprocal dx/dy = 1/(dy/dx) turns the equation the right way up; x sits alone (without a derivative) next to a dy term, which is the signal for linear-in-x rather than linear-in-y.
common_mistakes: Trying to separate the variables directly, missing that this equation is linear once inverted.
Losing the minus sign when moving x across, writing dx/dy + x = y + 1 (P = +1) instead of dx/dy − x = y + 1.

steps.label: Find the integrating factor
steps.margin_note: One mark. I.F. = e to the power ∫P dy always; here ∫P dy = −y.
steps.memory_tip: A constant P integrates to a straight line — ∫(−1)dy = −y, nothing more to it.

lines.text: The integrating factor is e to the power ∫P dy:

steps.why: The integrating-factor formula e to the power ∫P dy applies exactly the same way whether the equation is linear in x or in y; here P = −1 gives ∫P dy = −y directly.
common_mistakes: Writing the I.F. as eʸ by dropping the minus sign on P.
Confusing this P = −1 with a P(x) case and integrating with respect to x instead of y.

steps.label: Set up the integral for integration by parts
steps.margin_note: One mark. x·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dy is the standard linear solution formula, with x and y swapped.
steps.memory_tip: A polynomial times an exponential always calls for integration by parts, never a plain substitution.
lines: Hence the solution is x·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dy

lines.text: Here I.F. = e⁻ʸ and Q = y + 1:
A polynomial times an exponential needs

steps.why: Multiplying Q = y + 1 by the integrating factor e⁻ʸ gives the integral that must be evaluated; since it is a product of a polynomial and an exponential, integration by parts is the natural next step.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply Q by the integrating factor before integrating.
Attempting a substitution here instead of recognising that this integral needs integration by parts.
lines_compact: Hence the solution is x·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dy

steps.label: Integrate by parts and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. ∫e⁻ʸ(y+1)dy = −(y+2)e⁻ʸ + c by parts; divide through by e⁻ʸ to isolate x + y + 2.
steps.memory_tip: ∫(linear)·e⁻ʸ dy by parts always leaves one extra e⁻ʸ term beyond the direct product — check for it before finishing.

lines.text: By parts with u = y + 1, dv = e⁻ʸ dy, v = −e⁻ʸ:
The solution is x + y + 2 = ceʸ

steps.why: Integrating by parts with u = y+1 and dv = e⁻ʸdy gives −(y+2)e⁻ʸ after combining terms; moving the exponential across to the right side turns it into the standard multiplying factor ceʸ.
common_mistakes: Choosing dv = (y + 1)dy instead of dv = e⁻ʸdy, which does not simplify the integral.
Forgetting the extra −e⁻ʸ term that comes from ∫e⁻ʸdy inside the by-parts formula, and stopping at −(y + 1)e⁻ʸ + c.

lines_compact.text: The solution is x + y + 2 = ceʸ
